instructions: Put the sauerkraut in a colander and rinse it under cold water. Squeeze out as much water as you can. That should be about 1 1/2 cups.
Meanwhile, cut the bacon into 1-inch pieces. Halve the potatoes. Slice the onion and mince the garlic.

Set a large Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the bacon and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until it's crisp at the edges and the fat has melted into the pot. Transfer the bacon to a plate.

Raise the heat to medium-high. Add the bratwurst in a single layer and cook for 5 minutes, turning every minute or so, until browned on all sides. They won't be cooked through yet. Transfer them to the plate with the bacon.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion to the fat in the pot and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until soft. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds.
Pour in the wine and scrape up the browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Let it bubble for 3 minutes, until it's reduced by about half.
Add the sauerkraut, broth, juniper berries, cloves, bay leaves and pepper, and stir. Tuck in the potatoes, then lay the bacon and smoked pork chops on top.
Bring to a simmer, cover, and transfer the pot to the oven. Bake for 45 minutes.

Nestle the bratwurst into the sauerkraut, cover, and bake for 20 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the bratwurst is cooked through. You're cooking the bratwurst to 160°F in the middle, so if you have a thermometer, check it there. No thermometer? Cut into one: it's done when there's no pink left.
Take out the bay leaves. Taste the sauerkraut. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Mound the sauerkraut on a platter and put the potatoes around it. Slice the pork chops off the bone and lay them and the bratwurst on top. Serve with the Dijon mustard on the side.
method_notes: The sources agree on sauerkraut cooked slowly with smoked pork, sausages and potatoes, flavored with juniper and bay. They differ on the fat and the liquid: the lead uses bacon fat and beer, the Taste of France version uses butter and a whole bottle of Riesling, and Sainsbury's uses savoy cabbage and stock. I used the lead's layout, swapped the beer for dry white wine and broth as the Alsatian versions do, browned the sausages first, and rinsed the sauerkraut to keep it mild. The lead is rated 5 from 3 votes, so this is a fallback lead.
